fixes.row: The hope of the gospel, the calling, righteousness, salvation, eternal life; hope and being saved, the Savior (noun)
fixes.why: Jer 14:8 ('O Hope of Israel, its Savior in times of distress') is a Hebrew address to the LORD in a national lament (miqweh + moshia). Filed under 'the hope of the gospel ... the Savior' it is read as if it belonged to the NT gospel/salvation heading and is set beside Greek elpis verses (Col 1:23, Titus 2:13) as one hope. It is the example shown on the row's page for the 'Savior' tail, and the tail of the label exists largely to hold it. It already stands under Hope and Israel, where its own words and context are heard.
fixes.fix: Remove Jer 14:8 from the 'add' list of the gospel row (it stays in Hope and Israel). Keep 1 Tim 1:1, Titus 2:13, Rom 8:24 for the Savior / being-saved tail, which are Greek NT verses. If Doug wishes, Jer 14:8 could be added by hand to 'The LORD, God and hope' (Jer 14:7 and 14:9 name the LORD; divine-person placement is his decision).

fixes.row: The hope of the gospel, the calling, righteousness, salvation, eternal life; hope and being saved, the Savior (noun)
fixes.why: Acts 27:20 ('we abandoned all hope of being saved') is sailors in a storm hoping to survive the wreck. Under a row of the hope of the gospel, salvation and eternal life, beside 'hope and being saved', a reader takes it as the hope of salvation lost, which the verse does not say.
fixes.fix: Remove Acts 27:20 from the gospel row's 'add' list. It stays in 'Hope lost, perished ... without hope', where its label fits. The row's tail then reads 'hope and being saved' for Rom 8:24 alone, so it could be shortened to 'hope of salvation; hope and being saved, the Savior' once Jer 14:8 and Acts 27:20 are out.

fixes.why: The note puts three phrases in one breath, 'the hope of Israel' (Jer 14:8, 17:13; Acts 28:20), as if one phrase, though they are two different words (Hebrew miqweh, Greek elpis) and Ezra 10:2 and Ezek 37:11 are a third (tiqwah). It then sets the hope of Israel against 'the hope of the gospel (the row below)', which is not the row below and which opens the Hebrew verses with a Christian question before they are heard. Rules 4 and 5.
fixes.fix: Rewrite the note: 'Jer 14:8 and 17:13 call the LORD the hope of Israel (Hebrew miqweh); Acts 28:20 and 26:7 are Paul's Greek (elpis); Ezra 10:2 and Ezek 37:11 use tiqwah. These are different words, set side by side as written; the page does not say whether they are one hope. Whether the hope of Israel and the hope of the gospel are one or two, the page takes no side.' Drop '(the row below)'.

fixes.why: Ezra 10:2 is one of the four examples a reader sees first. Read cold it is 'unfaithful ... by marrying foreign women from the people of the land, yet ... there is hope for Israel', the opening of the dismissal of foreign wives. As a headline example it leads a hope hub with ethnic exclusion, with no context the page can give in one line.
fixes.fix: Change the row's lead to ['Jer.14.8','Jer.17.13','Acts.28.20','Ezek.37.11'] (Ezek 37:11 shows both hope and Israel), leaving Ezra 10:2 in the row's verses.

fixes.row: Hope with confidence and boldness, held fast, and shame (noun)
fixes.why: The note says 'hope set on Cush or on idols, whose people are ashamed (Isa 20:5, Jer 17:13)'. Jer 17:13 has no idols: it is 'O LORD, the hope of Israel, all who abandon You will be put to shame'. The note misreads the verse and sets Israel's God as the hope that fails, beside Cush. It also contrasts Rom 5:5 with Hebrew verses as 'hope that does not shame' versus hope that does, which is a tilt the verses do not make themselves.
fixes.fix: Replace the note with: 'Rom 5:5, hope that does not put to shame; Isa 20:5, those who made Cush their hope are ashamed; Jer 17:13, those who abandon the LORD, the hope of Israel, are put to shame. Set side by side as written.'

fixes.row: The hope of the righteous, the wicked, the godless, the poor and needy (noun)
fixes.why: Job 5:16 (Eliphaz), 8:13 (Bildad) and 11:20 (Zophar) are the friends' speeches; the text itself says at Job 42:7 that they did not speak rightly of God. Two of the first four examples shown are theirs, set in the same voice as Proverbs, so 'the hope of the godless will perish' reads as the book's own verdict. Missing context the text supplies.
fixes.fix: Add the note: 'Several of the Job verses (5:16, 8:13, 11:20) are spoken by Job's friends, of whom the LORD says at 42:7 that they have not spoken rightly of Him; Proverbs and the Psalms speak in their own voice.'

fixes.row: Hope lost, perished, uprooted, withered; without hope (noun)
fixes.why: Ps 9:18 says the hope of the oppressed will NOT be 'forever dashed'. It is here because of the verb, but under a label of hope lost it reads as the opposite of what it says, on a verse that is a promise to the poor.
fixes.fix: Remove Ps 9:18 from this row (add it to 'not_verses'); it remains in 'The hope of the righteous, the wicked, the godless, the poor and needy'.

fixes.row: Hope lost, perished, uprooted, withered; without hope (noun)
fixes.why: The first example is the exiles' complaint 'our hope has perished', the most-quoted line of Ezek 37, with nothing of the LORD's answer in 37:12-14. Most of the row is the speech of someone in distress (Job, Lamentations, the exiles), not the text's verdict; read without that, the row says that hope is lost.
fixes.fix: Add the note: 'Most of these are what someone in distress says, not what the text concludes: the LORD answers the exiles' words in Ezek 37:12-14.'

fixes.row: Hope and Israel; the nations, the islands will put their hope (verb)
fixes.why: Two different matters share one row and one note. (1) Israel is exhorted to hope in the LORD (Ps 130:7, 131:3), the faithful pray to the God of Israel (Ps 69:6), the disciples had hoped he would redeem Israel (Luke 24:21), the twelve tribes hope (Acts 26:7): hope WITH Israel. (2) The islands and the nations will put their hope (Isa 42:4, 51:5; Matt 12:21; Rom 15:12): hope of OTHERS. Under one label they read as a contrast of Israel with the nations. The note speaks of 'the hope of Israel and the hope of the gospel', which no verse in this row says (these are the noun row's phrases), and does not say that Matt 12:21 quotes Isa 42:4 while Rom 15:12 is a different quotation: Isa 11:10, where the Hebrew verb is 'seek', not 'hope'. The worker's own report assumes Rom 15:12 quotes Isa 42:4; it does not.
fixes.fix: Split into two rows. 'Hope and Israel' (Ps 130:7, Ps 131:3, Ps 69:6, Luke 24:21, Acts 26:7) with no note about the gospel, or a note: 'Israel is called to hope in the LORD (Ps 130:7, 131:3); Luke 24:21 and Acts 26:7 are the disciples' and Paul's words about Israel's hope.' And 'The nations, the islands will put their hope' (Isa 42:4, Isa 51:5, Matt 12:21, Rom 15:12) with the note: 'Matthew 12:21 quotes Isaiah 42:4; Romans 15:12 quotes Isaiah 11:10, where the Hebrew word is
. Who the nations hope in is in the verses; the page takes no side.'

fixes.row: Hope for what is not yet seen; hoped for one thing, and another came (verb)
fixes.why: One row carries two things the label itself joins with a semicolon: the NT's assurance of what is unseen (Rom 8:24-25, Heb 11:1) and the Hebrew Scriptures' hope disappointed (Job 30:26, Isa 59, Jer 8:15, 14:19, Isa 5:4). The first four examples shown pair Rom 8 and Heb 11 with Job 30:26, so the Hebrew verses are read as the failed hope the NT answers. Isa 5:4 is also the LORD speaking of his vineyard, not a person's hope.
fixes.fix: Split: 'Hope for what is not yet seen' (Rom 8:24, 8:25, Heb 11:1) and 'Hoped for one thing, and another came' (Job 30:26, Isa 59:9, 59:11, Jer 8:15, Jer 14:19, Isa 5:4), the latter with the note 'In Isa 5:4 it is the LORD who expected sweet grapes; the others are the people's words.'

fixes.row: Hope in the LORD, in God (verb)
fixes.why: Rule 4: the two Hebrew verbs are counted only where the Berean or MACULA renders them 'hope', so Ps 37:9 ('those who hope in the LORD') is in and Ps 25:3 ('none who wait for You will be put to shame') and Isa 40:31 ('those who wait upon the LORD') are out, though they are the same verbs in the same sense. A reader who looks for the best-known Hebrew verses on hope in the LORD will not find them and cannot tell why. One sense of a word presented as its whole.
fixes.fix: Add one line under the Hebrew verb rows: 'The Hebrew verbs yachal and qavah are also rendered "wait" in about forty-seven verses (for example Ps 27:14, Ps 25:3, Isa 40:31, Mic 7:7); those are not listed here.' (The word chips already show the counts; this says why.)

fixes.row: There is hope; hope and a future (noun)
fixes.why: Jer 29:11 is the third example shown and is the most quoted verse in the hub, with no context. The text supplies it (29:1, 29:10: the letter to the exiles in Babylon, seventy years); stripped of it the verse reads as a promise to any reader, which the page should not teach by omission. The report itself notes it but the hub does not.
fixes.fix: Add the note: 'Jer 29:11 and 31:17 are the LORD's word to the exiles of Judah (see 29:1, 29:10) and to Israel; Proverbs speaks of the one who finds wisdom.'

worker_points.point: 1. Hope and Israel (noun and verb) and the hope of the gospel: set side by side with a note that the page does not choose.
worker_points.why: The principle is right; the build is not. The gospel row now holds Jer 14:8 (OT verse under a gospel heading) and Acts 27:20 (a shipwreck). The Israel notes equate three phrases from two words and lead the Hebrew with a Christian question. The verb row mixes Israel's hope with the nations' under a note that does not describe it. See the fixes.

worker_points.point: 2. The hope of glory (Col 1:27, Rom 5:2): phrase as written, no gloss.
worker_points.why: Both verses show the phrase; the note names both and glosses neither. Christ and 'the glory of God' stay in the verses.
The label says only what the verses say, and the note states that the page does not say which is meant to be the hope. Acts 23:6, Paul's claim to a Pharisaic hope, stands as written.

worker_points.point: 4. The hope of righteousness (Gal 5:5) in the gospel row.
worker_points.why: The note names that readers part and the page takes no side. Gal 5:5 is also in the Spirit row; its verse shows 'through the Spirit' and 'the hope of righteousness'.

worker_points.point: 5. Divine persons by hand (Spirit, Christ, LORD, God Greek, Christ verb); Titus 2:13 in the Christ row; Jer 14:8 not in a God row.
worker_points.why: Labels say only 'named with', every placement is by hand, no rule infers a person. Titus 2:13 sits in the Christ row with the grammar left open. Jer 14:8 having no God row is consistent, though Jer 14:7 and 14:9 name the LORD, so Doug could add it. The real problem with Jer 14:8 is its place under the gospel row, which the fix removes.

worker_points.point: 6. Hebrew and Greek not pooled; miqweh and tiqwah are different words.
worker_points.why: True in the God/LORD rows. It fails in the Israel row (one note, 'the hope of Israel', over miqweh, elpis and tiqwah) and in the gospel row (Jer 14:8 miqweh beside elpis). See the fixes; the examples chip the lemma, but the note speaks as if there were one word.

worker_points.point: 7. Hope and the future puts Jer 29:11 beside Prov 23:18; no label claims to whom the promise is made.
worker_points.why: The label is fine, but the text supplies the addressee and the page leaves it out; a one-line note solves it without taking a side.

worker_points.point: 8. The nations, the islands (Isa 42:4, 51:5; Matt 12:21, Rom 15:12): Matthew and Romans quote Isa 42:4.
worker_points.why: Matt 12:21 quotes Isa 42:4; Rom 15:12 quotes Isa 11:10, whose Hebrew has the nations 'seek', not 'hope'. The worker's premise is wrong for Romans. The row must say which quotes which and must not bundle the nations with Israel.

worker_points.point: 9. Ordinary-sense rows (repayment, bribe, harvest, money; hoping to come; I hope you will understand) kept.
worker_points.why: They show the word is also everyday, and the shown examples (Rom 15:24, 1 Cor 16:7, 2 Cor 1:13, Phil 2:23) all show 'hope to'. Luke 23:8 (Herod hoping to see a sign) is correctly here. They do not dilute the theological verses, which come first.

worker_points.point: 10. Hebrew verbs: yachal and qavah count where MACULA glosses hope/expect, plus seven sense_keep verses where the Berean prints 'hope'. Is it right that the Berean's English decides?
worker_points.why: In each of the seven the original is the same verb as in the hope verses and the Berean's 'hope' is a fair reading, so keeping them is true to the text and the reasons are on record. The remaining risk is the reader who does not know that the same verbs are 'wait' elsewhere; one note covers it (see the fix on 'Hope in the LORD, in God').

missing.what: Jer 14:8 in 'The LORD, God and hope' (divine-person placement, Doug's decision): Jer 14:7-9 is addressed to the LORD; after it leaves the gospel row, the Hebrew row of the LORD as the hope of Israel would hold Jer 17:13 but not 14:8.

1 John 3:3 ('everyone who has this hope in Him purifies himself, just as Christ is pure'), a central NT hope verse, is in 'Every other use' only because the verse says 'Him'. The context names Christ in the same sentence; Doug could place it, with Job 13:15 and 2 Cor 1:10, by hand in 'Christ named with hope' (verb) or leave it.
Rom 8:20 ('in hope', of creation) is in 'Every other use' though it opens the same passage as Rom 8:24-25; consider listing it with the 'not yet seen' row.

summary: The hub is largely faithful, with good no-side notes and the divine persons by hand, but the merges damaged it: Jer 14:8 sits under a gospel heading, Acts 27:20 (a shipwreck) under salvation, and the Israel and nations verses share one note on a premise the text does not support (Rom 15:12 quotes Isa 11:10, not 42:4). With those moved or split, the Israel note rewritten by word, and the Job and Jer 29:11 notes added, all eleven seats could accept it.
